outcome: Since 26 January 2024 no event has settled or moved the bullet's named quantity (whether outer billiards relative to almost every convex polygon has unbounded orbits, or whether almost every orbit is periodic for a regular polygon). Two in-window events touch neighbouring questions: Belyi, Kanel-Belov, Rukhovich and Timorin extended the existence of aperiodic points to every regular N-gon with N not 3, 4 or 6 (version 2, 1 October 2024; this answers a different question from the bullet), and Sorrentino's preprint of 5 October 2026 proves unbounded orbits for a residual set of C¹ strictly convex centrally symmetric smooth tables, which the paper itself says does not cover polygons. The remaining in-window items concern other billiard systems (outer length, bouncing, contact, refractive, circular sectors, Ivrii-type periodicity).
problem_asks: (1) Show that outer billiards relative to almost every convex polygon has unbounded orbits, i.e. for almost every convex polygon some orbit of the outer billiard map is unbounded. This is the example the statement names. (2) The statement's umbrella 'many problems concerning an outer billiard' is not itemised in the statement. On my reading it points to the open-problems section of the Wikipedia outer billiards article, which as currently printed (maintenance-dated September 2026, with no citations) lists three further items: (2a) show that for a regular polygon almost every orbit is periodic; (2b) more broadly, characterise the structure of the set of periodic orbits relative to the typical convex polygon; (2c) understand the structure of periodic orbits relative to simple shapes in the hyperbolic plane. I could not retrieve the January 2024 wording of these items (the Wayback snapshot was refused), so the frozen wording may differ. 'Almost every' is not defined in any source I read: the measure on the space of convex polygons is unspecified, so 'almost every' in (1) and (2a) is unresolved as a measure-theoretic statement.

events.what_happened: Richard Evan Schwartz, 'Unbounded Orbits for Outer Billiards' (arXiv math/0702073, first posted 3 Feb 2007). Proves that outer billiards defined relative to the Penrose kite (a specific convex quadrilateral) has an unbounded orbit, answering the Moser–Neumann question affirmatively for that one polygon. Also shows an uncountable family of unbounded orbits. The arXiv comments say 65 pages, computer-aided proof, with an auxiliary program 'Billiard King' on the author's website.
events.revisions: v1 3 Feb 2007; v2 22 Feb 2007; v3 24 Feb 2007. The arXiv comments say the latest version is essentially the same as earlier ones, with minor improvements and typo fixes. No journal reference is shown on the arXiv page; I did not verify journal publication.
events.delivers: Unboundedness for one specific convex quadrilateral, the Penrose kite. Restriction: a single polygon, and the proof is computer-aided with exact integer arithmetic. It says nothing about almost every convex polygon.
events.remains: Problem (1) for every polygon other than the Penrose kite, including almost every convex polygon. Problems (2a) to (2c) entirely.
events.time_since_posted: about 19 years 8 months. Schwartz's own follow-ups build on it (see later_work_cites_it). I found no independent human verification of the computer-aided proof.
events.directly_checkable: The orbit is checkable by iterating the outer billiard map on the Penrose kite from a specific starting point with exact integer arithmetic. The arXiv comments point to the Billiard King program on the author's website. I did not open that program.
events.direction: Toward unboundedness, for the Penrose kite only. It answers the Moser–Neumann question affirmatively for that polygon.
events.object: A specific starting point p (shown as Figure 1.2 in the paper, per a search summary of Theorem 1.1) whose forward and backward outer billiard orbits are both defined and unbounded, for the Penrose kite (affinely a quadrilateral with vertices (0,1), (−1,0), (0,−1), (A,0), where A is the fractional part of √5, per a search summary). The point is explicit. Its unboundedness is established by the computer-aided argument.

events.what_happened: Richard Evan Schwartz, 'Outer Billiards on Kites' (arXiv 0709.1229, monograph). Its abstract says the first half proves that outer billiards has an unbounded orbit relative to any irrational kite, and the second half gives a sharp description of the unbounded set, both dynamically and by Hausdorff dimension.
events.revisions: v1 8 Sep 2007; v2 12 Jan 2008; v3 9 Feb 2008; v4 18 Feb 2008; v5 29 Jul 2008 (the current version on arXiv).
events.delivers: Unboundedness for every irrational kite, where an irrational kite is one not affinely equivalent to a quadrilateral with rational vertices (definition as reported in a search summary; I did not read the monograph's definition). Restriction: kites only. Rational kites are not covered by this statement. Kites are a symmetric subfamily of convex quadrilaterals, so this is not a statement about polygons in general. My inference, not stated in the sources, is that kites form a lower-dimensional family in the space of convex quadrilaterals, so this result does not by itself bear on the measure in problem (1).
events.remains: Problem (1) for every convex polygon that is not an irrational kite, including almost every convex polygon under any reasonable measure. Rational kites. Problems (2a) to (2c).
events.time_since_posted: about 19 years. Schwartz's own 2011 paper and later search results cite this line of work. I found no independent verification.
events.direction: Toward unboundedness, for irrational kites only.
events.object: Existence of an unbounded orbit for each irrational kite. The construction is not explicit in the abstract. The monograph uses computer checks in places (per a search snippet: checks that some 4-dimensional convex integral polytopes have disjoint interiors). I did not read the monograph body.

events.what_happened: Chris Culter's theorem, that every convex polygonal outer billiard has a periodic trajectory, as written up expositorily by Serge Tabachnikov, 'A proof of Culter's theorem on the existence of periodic orbits in polygonal outer billiards' (arXiv 0706.1003, first posted 7 June 2007). Per a search snippet, the note was published in Geometriae Dedicata 129 (2007), 83–87. Culter's result was obtained as a participant in the 2004 Penn State REU, per the same snippet.
events.revisions: Single arXiv version as shown on the abstract page. The journal version is from a search snippet, not opened.
events.delivers: Existence of at least one periodic orbit for every convex polygon in the Euclidean plane. Existence only. It says nothing about the structure of periodic orbits, their measure, or unboundedness. Per a search snippet the note assumes no parallel sides for ease of exposition.
events.remains: Problems (2a) to (2c). Problem (1) entirely (existence of a periodic orbit does not decide boundedness).

checked_by.qualification: Established billiards researcher, co-author of the Bialy et al. open-problems list and of the Tabachnikov monograph on billiards and geometry (per the search results).
checked_by.what_they_did: Published an expository proof of Culter's theorem; it appeared in Geometriae Dedicata (2007) per a search snippet.

events.directly_checkable: The periodic orbit is checkable in principle by iterating the map on a given polygon; the note's argument is short (about four pages per a search snippet).
events.direction: Neither toward nor against unboundedness. It shows that periodic orbits always exist for convex polygons in the Euclidean plane.

events.what_happened: Dmitry Dolgopyat and Bassam Fayad, 'Unbounded orbits for semicircular outer billiard', Annales Henri Poincaré 10 (2009), 357–375. The outer billiard around a semicircle has unbounded orbits (an open set escaping to infinity, per a 2025 arXiv citation). Their proof is robust, also working for circular caps close to a semicircle and for regions from cutting a disk nearly in half. The Wikipedia article gives 2008 as the date of the result; the PDF on Dolgopyat's UMD page has metadata creation date 9 September 2008.
events.revisions: Published Annales Henri Poincaré 2009. The preprint's arXiv status was not found. The date 2008 rests on the Wikipedia text and the PDF metadata; I could not read the PDF body.
events.delivers: Unbounded orbits for the semicircle and nearby caps. Restriction: a piecewise smooth table that is not a polygon. The paper does not decide any polygon case.
events.remains: Problem (1) for all convex polygons. Problems (2a) to (2c).

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper in 2009 (per journal citations found in search results).

events.direction: Toward unboundedness, for a non-polygonal piecewise smooth table.
events.object: An open ball of initial points (around the semicircle) whose orbits escape to infinity. The existence is established by the paper's argument. The object is not explicit in the sources I read.

events.what_happened: Richard Evan Schwartz, 'Outer Billiards and the Pinwheel Map' (arXiv 1004.3025, first posted 18 April 2010). Establishes a bijection between orbits of a polygonal outer billiard system and orbits of a simpler pinwheel map. One consequence is that the outer billiard has unbounded orbits if and only if the pinwheel map does.
events.revisions: v1 18 Apr 2010 as shown on the abstract page; no later versions examined.
events.delivers: An equivalence reducing unboundedness for a polygonal outer billiard to unboundedness for the pinwheel map. It settles nothing by itself: no polygon is shown to have, or lack, unbounded orbits.
events.remains: Problem (1) and problems (2a) to (2c). The equivalence is a tool for them, not a solution.
events.direction: Neutral on the bullet. It is a reduction that the author expects to help with the main questions about polygonal outer billiards.

events.what_happened: Richard Evan Schwartz, 'Outer Billiards on the Penrose Kite: Compactification and Renormalization' (arXiv 1102.4635, first posted 22 February 2011). Gives a detailed analysis of outer billiards on the Penrose kite. One result is that the union of the unbounded orbits has Hausdorff dimension 1. The abstract says the compactification and renormalization results are computer-aided, with finitely many calculations in exact integer arithmetic.
events.revisions: v1 only, 22 Feb 2011, per the abstract page.
events.delivers: For the Penrose kite only: the unbounded orbits form a set of Hausdorff dimension 1. The abstract does not say whether that dimension statement itself is computer-aided.
events.remains: Problem (1) for every polygon other than the Penrose kite. Problems (2a) to (2c).
events.direction: Toward unboundedness, for the Penrose kite only. It refines the picture of the set of unbounded orbits.
events.object: The set of unbounded orbits for the Penrose kite, analysed through a three-dimensional compactification. The object is a set of orbits, not a single explicit point.

events.what_happened: Filipp Rukhovich, 'Outer billiards' (arXiv 1505.06332). The abstract of v3 (24 Nov 2017) says it treats outer, or dual, billiards outside regular polygons, with periodic points for strictly convex tables and regular n-gons with n = 3, 4, 6, 8, 12. Its main results are: an aperiodic point for the regular octagon and the regular dodecagon; full measure of periodic points for the regular octagon; and a list of all possible periods for the regular octagon. The arXiv comments say 60 pages, in Russian.
events.revisions: v1 23 May 2015; v2 24 Jun 2015; v3 24 Nov 2017. I did not check whether v1 or v2 contain the octagon or dodecagon claims. I have dated this event to v3, the earliest version I verified carries them. If v1 already carries them, the date should move to 23 May 2015.
events.delivers: For the regular octagon only: periodic points form a set of full measure, so almost every orbit is periodic. This is an instance of problem (2a) for n = 8. The aperiodic-point claim concerns the octagon and dodecagon but is not a measure statement.
events.remains: Problem (2a) for every regular n-gon other than the octagon (the dodecagon full-measure claim is a separate event). Problem (1). Problems (2b) and (2c).

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the combined treatment 'Outer billiards outside regular polygons: tame case' (Izvestiya RAN, Ser. Mat. 86 (2022), 105–160; English Izvestiya: Mathematics 86:3, 508–559), per a search snippet. The octagon Doklady paper (2018, vol. 98, no. 1, pp. 334–337) is also cited in a search snippet. I did not open either journal page.

events.direction: Toward a measure-theoretic periodicity statement for the octagon, which is what problem (2a) asks for that one polygon.
events.object: Periodic points of the regular octagon outer billiard, described in full with their periods (listed explicitly). The full-measure statement is over the complement of the octagon's outer region. The aperiodic point is claimed to exist but is not described in the abstract.

events.what_happened: Filipp Rukhovich, 'Outer billiards outside regular octagon: set of full measure and an aperiodic point' (arXiv 1712.01130, first posted 4 December 2017). Describes all periodic points and their periods for the regular octagon outer billiard, proves that periodic points form a set of full measure outside the octagon, and finds an aperiodic point. This restates the octagon claims of the event rukhovich-2017-octagon-full-measure-v3 in a standalone preprint.
events.delivers: For the regular octagon only: full measure of periodic points, so almost every orbit is periodic. Instance of problem (2a) for n = 8.
events.remains: Problem (2a) for every other regular polygon. Problem (1). Problems (2b) and (2c).
events.direction: Toward a measure-theoretic periodicity statement for the octagon.
events.object: Periodic points of the regular octagon outer billiard, with all periods listed. Aperiodic point found, not described in the abstract.

events.what_happened: Filipp Rukhovich, 'Outer billiards outside regular dodecagon: computer proof of periodicity of almost all orbits and existence of an aperiodic point' (arXiv 1809.03791, first posted 11 September 2018). Proves an aperiodic point exists for the outer billiard outside the regular dodecagon, and that almost all orbits are periodic, with all possible periods listed explicitly. The proof rests on facts established by a computer program written by the author, run with absolute accuracy. Per a search snippet, the paper was published in Doklady (vol. 485, no. 4, 2019, pp. 415–421) and the combined version in Izvestiya 2022.
events.delivers: For the regular dodecagon only: almost every orbit is periodic (problem (2a) instance for n = 12), proved by a computer-assisted argument with the author's own program. Also an aperiodic point exists for n = 12.
events.remains: Problem (2a) for every regular polygon other than the octagon and dodecagon. Problem (1). Problems (2b) and (2c).

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the result in Doklady 2019 and in the 2022 Izvestiya combined treatment (both per search snippets; I did not open either).

machine_checked.system: Author's own computer program (not a proof assistant)

events.directly_checkable: The computations are checkable only by re-running the author's program, which the abstract says gives exact results. I found no independent reimplementation.
events.doubts: The argument depends on one author-written program. I found no independent reimplementation or re-verification in my searches. This is a fact about the verification, not a finding that the result is wrong.
events.direction: Toward a measure-theoretic periodicity statement, for the dodecagon.
events.object: Periodic structure of the regular dodecagon outer billiard, with all periods listed. The aperiodic point is claimed but not described in the abstract.

events.what_happened: Gutkin and Simányi, 'Dual polygonal billiards and necklace dynamics' (Communications in Mathematical Physics 143 (1992), 431–449). Shows that for outer billiards, orbits about quasi-rational polygons are bounded and orbits about rational polygons are periodic. The 2026 Park preprint restates this result, per its abstract.
events.delivers: Boundedness of all orbits for quasi-rational polygons (which include all regular n-gons and all rational polygons), and periodicity for rational polygons. Restriction: a special arithmetic class. This is the opposite behaviour to problem (1) on that class, but says nothing about polygons outside it.
events.remains: Problem (1) for all polygons outside the quasi-rational class. The sources do not say how large that class is in the bullet's measure. Problems (2a) to (2c).
events.direction: Toward boundedness (and periodicity for rational polygons). Cuts against problem (1) for the quasi-rational class.

events.what_happened: A. Shaidenko and F. Vivaldi, 'Global stability of a class of discontinuous dual billiards' (Comm. Math. Phys. 110 (1987), 625–640), per a search snippet. The result is that all orbits are bounded for outer billiards around a regular polygon, and per search summaries it extends to a class containing the regular polygons. I did not open the paper; the citation details come from a later paper's reference list.
events.delivers: Boundedness of all orbits for regular polygons (per a search summary, not verified against the paper). Restriction: regular polygons and possibly a wider class. Says nothing about unbounded orbits on typical polygons.
events.remains: Problem (1) and problems (2a) to (2c) for polygons outside the stated class.
events.direction: Toward boundedness, for regular polygons.

events.what_happened: Kanel-Belov, Rukhovich, Timorin and Zgurskii, 'Aperiodic points for dual billiards' (arXiv 2311.09643, v1). The abstract says the Euclidean dual billiard (the same map as the outer billiard) outside a regular N-gon or 2N-gon, for odd N > 3, has aperiodic points.
events.revisions: v1 16 Nov 2023; v2 1 Oct 2024; v3 15 Jan 2025; v4 25 Feb 2025; v5 4 May 2026. See the event belyi-et-al-2024-v2-all-N.
events.delivers: Existence of aperiodic points for regular n-gons with n odd and n at least 5, and for regular n-gons with n ≡ 2 (mod 4) and n at least 10 (the 2N-gon case). Existence only. Says nothing about the measure of periodic points or about unboundedness. Covers no regular polygon with 4 dividing n.
events.remains: Regular n-gons with 4 dividing n (the octagon and dodecagon were already done by Rukhovich; the rest were not). Problem (1). Problems (2a) to (2c).
events.direction: Existence of aperiodic points for these regular polygons. This shows periodicity is not universal there, but does not address almost every orbit.
events.object: An aperiodic point: a point whose outer billiard iterates are all defined and pairwise distinct. The v1 abstract does not say whether the point is explicit or non-constructive. The argument in v1 is not described in the abstract.

events.what_happened: Anastasiia Sharipova, 'Ivrii's conjecture for some cases in outer and symplectic billiards' (arXiv 2402.18782, v1 29 Feb 2024). Proves the (2n+1, n) and (2n, n−1) periodic cases of Ivrii's conjecture for planar outer billiards, and gives new geometric proofs of the 3- and 4-periodic cases for outer and symplectic billiards.
events.revisions: A v2 exists (per a search result link). Its date was not checked.
events.delivers: Periodic-orbit results for planar outer billiards in the Ivrii family: the (2n+1, n) and (2n, n−1) cases. The abstract does not say whether the tables in question are polygons or smooth curves, and says nothing about unboundedness or about the measure of periodic orbits.
events.remains: Problems (2b) and (2c) as stated, and problem (2a). Problem (1) entirely.
events.direction: Periodicity results in a family of periodic-orbit conjectures. No direction for problem (1).

events.what_happened: The same arXiv paper in later versions, retitled 'Aperiodic points for outer billiards' by v4 with Anton Belyi as an author. Version 2 (1 Oct 2024) abstract: 'Euclidean outer billiard on a regular polygon (that is not a triangle, square or a hexagon) has aperiodic points', which 'answers a question of R. Schwartz posed at ICM 2022'. Version 5 (4 May 2026, the current version) states the main theorem: 'Outer billiard on any regular N-gon with N>4 and N≠6 has aperiodic points'. Before this, a seminar talk by Timorin on 7 May 2024 (HUJI, title 'Aperiodic points for outer billiards', joint work with Kanel-Belov, Rukhovich and Zgurskii) said the answer was affirmative for N not divisible by 4 and that the method uses scissor-congruence invariants rather than self-similarity. Under the rule for dating, a talk is dated to the write-up, so the talk is not a separate event. The 4 dividing n cases first appear in the verified dated versions with v2.
events.revisions: v1 16 Nov 2023 (odd N and 2N-gons, title 'Aperiodic points for dual billiards'); v2 1 Oct 2024 (same title, broadened abstract); v3 15 Jan 2025; v4 25 Feb 2025 (title 'Aperiodic points for outer billiards'); v5 4 May 2026 (about 4.2 MB; no changelog found). What changed between v4 and v5 was not identified. The date 1 Oct 2024 is the earliest dated version I could verify that carries the 4 dividing n cases. A version or talk between 7 May 2024 and 1 Oct 2024 could carry them, which would move the date earlier, but still inside the window.
events.delivers: Existence of aperiodic points for every regular N-gon with N not 3, 4 or 6, i.e. N = 5 and all N ≥ 7 (v5 main theorem: N>4, N≠6). This completes Schwartz's ICM 2022 question for regular polygons. Restriction: existence of aperiodic points only. It says nothing about the measure of periodic points or about unboundedness.
events.remains: Problem (2a) (almost every orbit periodic) is not decided: existence of aperiodic points is a different quantity. Problem (1) entirely. Problems (2b) and (2c). The abstract does not say the measure of aperiodic points is zero or positive.
events.time_since_posted: about 24 months from v2; about 35 months from v1. I found no public review or verification.
events.direction: Existence of aperiodic points for all regular N-gons with N not 3, 4, 6. Periodicity is not universal for these polygons, which cuts against a universal periodicity claim. It does not touch almost every orbit.
events.object: An aperiodic point for each regular N-gon with N not 3, 4, 6: a point whose outer billiard iterates are all defined and pairwise distinct. The method uses scissor-congruence invariants (Sah–Arnoux–Fathi and Hadwiger–Glur, per the July 2024 talk abstract), not dynamical self-similarity. The abstract does not say whether the point is explicit.
people: Valery Zgurskii (co-author of v1; acknowledged as a member at an earlier stage in v5)

events.what_happened: Andrey Gogolev, Levi Keck, Kevin Lewis, 'Bouncing Outer Billiards' (arXiv 2410.17985, 23 Oct 2024). Introduces three-dimensional relatives of the Neumann–Moser outer billiard. Proves that a bouncing outer billiard on a smooth convex body has at least four 1-parameter families of fixed points, and describes the dynamics on a segment fully. Numerical experiments on shapes including the square and an ellipse suggest complicated, non-ergodic behaviour. A search snippet lists it as published in Arnold Mathematical Journal in 2025; not verified.
events.revisions: Single version, v1 23 Oct 2024 (per the abstract page).
events.delivers: Nothing about the planar outer billiard on polygons. The system is a three-dimensional bouncing map, so this is a discarded event for problem (1) and problems (2a) to (2c).
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks.
events.direction: None for this bullet.

events.what_happened: Lael Edwards-Costa, 'Outer length billiards on polygons' (arXiv 2510.11869, 13 Oct 2025). Studies the 'outer with length' billiard on polygonal tables, a different system from the classical outer billiard (which uses area). Describes the behaviour of orbits far from the table and poses conjectures about an escaping orbit when the table is a square. The abstract says these are conjectures.
events.revisions: Single version as shown on the abstract page. A search snippet also mentions a companion paper on smooth tables (arXiv 2510.08370); not opened.
events.delivers: Nothing proved about the classical outer billiard. It is a different system on polygons. Its conjectures about escaping orbits for the square are about the outer length billiard. Discarded for problem (1) and (2a) to (2c).
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks for the classical outer billiard.
events.direction: None for this bullet. The conjectured escaping orbit for a square concerns a different system.

events.what_happened: Zaicun Li, 'Elliptic islands and zero measure escaping orbits in a class of outer billiards' (arXiv 2506.18433, 23 Jun 2025). Studies outer billiards around a class of circular sectors. For semi-discs, proves elliptic islands occupying a positive proportion of the plane, which with known results shows coexistence of stability and diffusion. Shows there is a countable family of circular sectors for which the outer billiard has zero measure of escaping orbits.
events.delivers: Results on circular sectors and semi-discs, not on polygons. The escaping-orbit results concern a countable family of sectors and the measure of escaping orbits for them. Discarded for problem (1): sectors are not polygons, and the paper says nothing about unbounded orbits as such.
events.remains: Problem (1) for all convex polygons. Problems (2a) to (2c).
events.direction: Measure of escaping orbits for non-polygonal tables: positive for elliptic islands, zero for a countable family. Silent about polygons.

events.what_happened: Misha Bialy and Serge Tabachnikov, 'Remarks on the outer length billiards' (arXiv 2603.05998, 6 Mar 2026). For outer length billiards: proves 3- and 4-periodic versions of Ivrii's conjecture; for every period n ≥ 3 constructs a functional space of billiard tables whose invariant curves consist of n-periodic points; for n = 4, parametrises centrally symmetric tables by one-variable functions.
events.delivers: Periodic-orbit results for outer length billiards. The abstract never says that the system is the classical planar outer billiard, so this is a discarded event for problem (1) and (2a) to (2c).
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks for the classical outer billiard.
events.direction: Periodicity results for a different system. None for this bullet.

events.what_happened: Jaewoo Park, 'Polygonal Refractive Outer Billiards' (arXiv 2608.02936, 3 Aug 2026). Introduces the refractive outer billiard about a convex polygon. Its abstract restates Gutkin–Simányi (1992: orbits about quasi-rational polygons bounded, about rational polygons periodic) and Tabachnikov–Culter (2007: every convex polygonal outer billiard admits a periodic trajectory) and says the authors generalise both results to the refractive setting.
events.delivers: Generalisation of the boundedness and periodicity results to the refractive system. A different system from the classical outer billiard. Discarded for problem (1) and (2a) to (2c), but it is the most recent paper I found that treats polygonal outer billiard dynamics.
events.remains: Problem (1) and (2a) to (2c) for the classical system.
events.direction: Restates the bounded and periodic results for the refractive system. None for the bullet.

events.what_happened: Ana Chávez-Caliz and Connor Jackman, 'Outer Contact Billiards' (arXiv 2608.19393, 19 Aug 2026). Introduces an odd-dimensional counterpart to outer symplectic billiards, obtained by projectivising them. Proves the map generates contactomorphisms, that quadratic tables in RP³ are completely integrable, and rigidity results for periodic orbits (no 3-periodic orbits; among quadratic tables only one admits 4-periodic orbits).
events.revisions: Single version as shown on the abstract page.
events.delivers: Results about a different system in contact geometry. Discarded for problem (1) and (2a) to (2c).
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks for the classical outer billiard.
events.direction: None for this bullet.

events.what_happened: Alfonso Sorrentino (Università di Roma Tor Vergata and the Institute for Advanced Study), 'Unbounded orbits in C¹-generic centrally symmetric strictly convex outer billiards' (arXiv 2610.06418, first posted 5 Oct 2026, single author). The paper shows that for a residual set of centrally symmetric, strictly convex C¹ tables, given as support functions, the outer billiard map has unbounded orbits escaping to infinity. The set includes tables arbitrarily C¹-close to disks or ellipses. It presents this as an affirmative answer, in the strictly convex C¹ setting, to the Moser–Neumann question. Its introduction cites Schwartz's Question 6.9 (asking whether a strictly convex or C¹ domain with unbounded outer billiard orbits exists) and says it answers that. Key ingredients: a rigidity theorem for tables whose radius-of-curvature measure is purely singular, and Mather's diffusing mechanism in a Birkhoff region of instability.
events.revisions: Single version v1, 5 Oct 2026 (per the abstract page). No later version as of 13 Oct 2026.
events.delivers: Unbounded orbits for a residual set of centrally symmetric, strictly convex C¹ tables. Restrictions: smooth boundary (C¹), strictly convex, centrally symmetric. Polygons are excluded: the introduction's remark 1.4(i) says polygons are neither C¹ nor strictly convex. The introduction also says the model 'can be extended to polygons' with suitable adaptations (read from a summarised fetch; not confirmed against the raw text), but no polygon result is claimed.
events.remains: Problem (1) for convex polygons (not addressed). Problems (2a) to (2c). Non-centrally-symmetric tables and tables that are not strictly convex or not C¹ are also outside this result.
events.direction: Toward unboundedness, for the smooth strictly convex class. Silent about convex polygons. Whether this counts toward problem (1) depends on whether the judging pass reads the Moser–Neumann question as the bullet's polygon question or as the general question.
events.object: No explicit table or orbit. Existence is a residual-set (Baire-category) statement, built using Mather's diffusing mechanism in a Birkhoff region of instability, after a rigidity theorem for tables with purely singular radius-of-curvature measure. The escaping orbits are not written down explicitly in the abstract.

disputes.summary: A search summary reported that Wikipedia dates Schwartz's Penrose kite result to 1982, while the arXiv preprint is dated 2007 (math/0702073, first posted 3 Feb 2007). The Wikipedia text I fetched did not state a year for that result, so I could not confirm the 1982 date from the page. The 2007 date is the one supported by the primary source.

Dolgopyat and Fayad's semicircle result is dated 2008 in the Wikipedia text and 2009 in the Annales Henri Poincaré journal reference. The PDF metadata gives 9 September 2008 as its creation date. These are consistent with a 2008 preprint and 2009 publication, but the preprint's arXiv status was not found.

summary: The bullet's named question, whether outer billiards relative to almost every convex polygon has an unbounded orbit, is still open on every source I read, and no event in the window decides it. The polygon results that do exist are all for specific polygons or special families: Schwartz's Penrose kite (arXiv math/0702073, February 2007), and his irrational-kite monograph (arXiv 0709.1229, September 2007 to July 2008). The irrational-kite result is for a symmetric subfamily of quadrilaterals, and the sources do not define the measure for 'almost every', so I did not treat it as settling the bullet. For problem (2a), periodicity for almost every orbit, the octagon (Rukhovich, 2015 to 2017; standalone 4 December 2017) and the dodecagon (Rukhovich, 11 September 2018, computer-assisted with the author's own program) are settled before the window, and the other regular polygons are not. In-window, the event closest to the bullet's neighbourhood is Belyi, Kanel-Belov, Rukhovich, Timorin and Zgurskii's paper on aperiodic points. Its v1 (16 November 2023, odd N and 2N-gons) predates the window. Its 4 dividing n cases first appear in the verified dated version v2 (1 October 2024), and the current v5 (4 May 2026) states N > 4, N ≠ 6. That is existence of aperiodic points, which does not decide almost every orbit, so I recorded it as a different question. The main recent item is Sorrentino's preprint of 5 October 2026 (arXiv 2610.06418), which proves unbounded orbits for a residual set of centrally symmetric strictly convex C¹ tables. It is one week old, single-author and unreviewed. Its introduction says polygons are neither C¹ nor strictly convex, so polygons are not covered, although a remark says the model 'can be extended to polygons' with suitable adaptations; I could read that only through a summarised fetch. The AI search found one AI disclosure in the mathematics: Sorrentino's title block says 'AI Disclosure: A near-final draft of this paper was proofread with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic),' and, per the same fetch, that Claude helped generate the TikZ code for the figures and the author takes full responsibility. This is proofreading and figure code, not load-bearing mathematics, so it is not in ai.systems. The quote comes from a summarised fetch of the HTML page, and I did not check it against the raw text. No AI-generated or AI-assisted result on outer billiards was found. The other AI leads were off-target: a Claude-generated simulation repository for a dissipative outer billiard on a flower-shaped table (undated, simulation only, a different map); Sra's 'GPT, the Counterexample Machine' (arXiv 2608.29595), whose text I read except for part of Appendix A.2 and which contains no billiards hits; and a GPT or AlphaEvolve search that found nothing. Where a call was close, the main one is the date of the 4 dividing n cases in Belyi et al. (I used 1 October 2024, the earliest verified version; a talk on 7 May 2024 covered only N not divisible by 4). The second is the date of Rukhovich's octagon full-measure claim (I used 24 November 2017, the earliest verified version; the 23 May 2015 first version was not checked). A third is whether Sorrentino's smooth result should count toward the bullet at all. Several statements about the wider literature come only from search summaries I could not verify against the primary text: that Dolgopyat and Fayad remark that unbounded orbits are believed for almost all N-gons, and that it is unknown whether a polygon has a positive-measure set of unbounded orbits; that Schwartz's ICM 2022 survey poses a polygon question; and Question 6.7 versus 6.9. The January 2024 Wikipedia wording of the open-problems list could not be retrieved. The Wayback snapshot was refused.
competing_reading: A reading in which Sorrentino's 5 October 2026 result counts toward the bullet: the Moser–Neumann question as stated in the Wikipedia article and in Sorrentino's introduction is 'Is there a convex table for which the outer billiard has an unbounded orbit?'. An affirmative answer for a residual set of smooth strictly convex tables answers that question in its general form, and the bullet's polygon version is a sharper target. A reading in which it does not count: the bullet names convex polygons, the paper says polygons are excluded because they are neither C¹ nor strictly convex, and the bullet's measure over polygons is a different claim from a residual set in a space of smooth support functions. On the Belyi et al. paper: a reading in which it moves the bullet is that aperiodic points for all regular N-gons is a periodicity statement for each polygon, so the bullet's 'periodic structure for a regular polygon' is affected. A reading in which it does not is that existence of aperiodic points says nothing about the measure of periodic points, which is what the bullet asks for. On the kites: a reading in which the irrational-kite result bears on 'almost every convex polygon' is that irrational kites are full-measure within the kites. The reading against it is that kites are a lower-dimensional family among convex polygons, so the result does not carry over to the measure in the bullet.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The January 2024 wording of the Wikipedia open-problems list for outer billiards, to confirm the frozen bullets and which of them the umbrella 'many problems' covers. (2) The text of Schwartz's ICM 2022 survey, to find the question the bullet cites (Question 6.7 versus 6.9) and its precise measure. (3) A definition of 'almost every' for convex polygons in the source the bullet relies on. (4) The full text of Sorrentino 2610.06418, in particular its remark on extending the model to polygons and its exact AI disclosure, and any independent expert reading in the weeks after 5 October 2026. (5) The version history of arXiv 2311.09643, in particular whether v2 or a talk before October 2024 first carried the 4 dividing n cases, and what changed between v4 and v5. (6) The Dolgopyat–Fayad PDF text for the statements about almost every N-gon and positive-measure unbounded orbits. (7) The Rukhovich v1 (23 May 2015) text, to fix the date of the octagon full-measure claim.
